title: Agriculture a 'sign' of the times? - The Western Producer
description:
There I was, when I stumbled across a sign near someone’s front door that read, “A flower does not think of competing with the flower next to it.
I am learning something new every day in the vast diversity that agriculture offers, but it has also taken away some of the romanticism you see on inspirational posters, social media and movies.
Social media has a way of constantly telling us how horrible life is.
Nature and agriculture have a way of bringing us back to the land and admiring what is in front of us.
In the bigger picture, that’s what the sign really meant.
text:
Thanks Western Producer, for making me a Debbie Downer.

I speak of course in jest, but the thought did strike my mind while I was on one of the many leisurely neighbourhood walks I take after being chained to my laptop all day writing stories and doing research.

There I was, when I stumbled across a sign near someone’s front door that read, “A flower does not think of competing with the flower next to it. It just blooms.”

However, instead of the inspirational message giving me the warm and fuzzies about living in a society in which we are supportive of each other, what instantly entered my brain was the agronomic equivalent of Ebenezer Scrooge kicking the uplifting crutch from under Tiny Tim.

If I have learned anything from the numerous field days I have attended in southern Alberta, it is that plants are in a constant fight for survival with their neighbouring brethren. Row spacing for seeding, a careful formula of inputs such as nitrogen, sunlight, available moisture — the list of what crops compete for in order to truly “bloom” in the at-times harsh drought conditions of the area goes on and on.

I am learning something new every day in the vast diversity that agriculture offers, but it has also taken away some of the romanticism you see on inspirational posters, social media and movies.

Those testosterone-filled spaghetti Westerns we of the Gen X enjoyed? Malarkey, at least as far as being bitten on the dusty trail by a rattlesnake in the Wild West. Sucking the poison out, cutting around the wound, suctioning it out or applying a rough tourniquet, which are techniques often found on the big screen, are definitely no-nos.

“Unless you really don’t like that arm for whatever reason,” still echoes in my head from a presentation from rattlesnake expert Sheri Monk during a Farming Smarter field day in June.

However, for the less high-stakes stuff, cannot an “ignorance is bliss” approach help us a little in not being in a constant state of worry?

Social media has a way of constantly telling us how horrible life is. Nature and agriculture have a way of bringing us back to the land and admiring what is in front of us.

In the bigger picture, that’s what the sign really meant.

RRI.CO.ID, Jakarta – Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto received Timor-Leste counterpart José Ramos-Horta and several Nobel laureates at the Merdeka Palace in Jakarta on Friday, August 28, 2026. During the meeting, the two leaders discussed ways to enhance cooperation, including collaboration between Nobel laureates and Indonesian researchers and academics.

"There is, I think, much more potential to explore going forward, especially since these Nobel laureates come from various backgrounds. Some are in biology, some in physics, and so on," the country's Minister of Culture Fadli Zon said in a statement following the meeting, as quoted from the Indonesian Presidential Secretariat on Friday.

Head of the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) Arif Satria explained that such collaboration would be an important foundation for strengthening Indonesia’s domestic research ecosystem. According to him, President Prabowo emphasized that the collaboration should be realized as soon as possible.

"It is extremely important for the Nobel laureates to provide inspiration and then become part of the ecosystem for strengthening research talent in Indonesia. The president also very much hopes that this collaboration can be carried out as soon as possible," Arif explained.

Arif said BRIN had previously undertaken a similar collaboration in developing metal-organic frameworks with Japanese Nobel laureate Susumu Kitagawa. According to him, the cooperation involved establishing a sister lab in Indonesia focused on developing natural gas-related technologies.

"As I have previously explained, this Japanese Nobel laureate went on to establish a sister lab in Indonesia. The sister lab in Indonesia is now preparing to develop a way to produce natural gas at lower pressure using the findings from the Nobel laureate’s research," he said.

In addition, Arif said that the laureates had previously visited a conservation area in Sumatra's Lampung province. This also became a topic of discussion at the meeting, particularly on efforts to strengthen nature conservation in Indonesia.

"The president also has a very strong commitment to further strengthening the protection of Indonesia’s flora and fauna. Those were some of the points conveyed by the president earlier," he said.

During the meeting, Prabowo also outlined several of Indonesia’s strategic programs, ranging from food security to the development of fishing villages. According to Arif, the President also shared Indonesia’s experience in implementing the Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) program.

"The president also discussed various strategic programs related to food security, our experience with MBG, and he also continued to emphasize his commitment to developing fishing villages," he explained.

In addition to discussing research development and national strategic programs, President Prabowo urged BRIN to continue creating innovations to address Indonesia’s potential disaster risks. One innovation receiving attention is the development of earthquake-resistant modular house prototypes, which have been built since 2021–2022.

"The president said earlier that Indonesia is located in the 'Ring of Fire', with many areas highly vulnerable to disasters. Therefore, he said that this requires research and technological innovations to address and anticipate these risks, as well as to continue providing solutions so that such disasters can be prevented from occurring in Indonesia," Arif concluded.

HONG KONG, Aug. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- A major event for the global energy sector—the International Gas Union’s (IGU) 2026 Council Meeting and “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit—will take place in Hong Kong from 26 to 29 October 2026, with The Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (Towngas) serving as the host organisation. Leaders of major global energy corporations, regional government officials, experts, scholars and representatives of international organisations will assemble in Hong Kong to examine global energy security, the evolution to a green and low-emission economy and the roadmap for achievable, just and sustainable development.

IGU is the world’s most influential and authoritative international non-profit membership organisation of the global Gas industry, with members accounting for over 90% of the global Gas market. The decision to host this Council Meeting and Summit in Hong Kong, with Towngas as the host organisation, not only accentuates the international Gas community’s recognition of Hong Kong as an international metropolis and a green finance hub but, also, highlights Towngas’s significant contribution to the energy evolution and to IGU itself.

Amid drastic shifts across the international landscape, global supply chains restructuring, and low-emission energy choices, the future development of the global Gas industry, including that of natural gas, has attracted considerable attention. Over the course of a four-day series of meetings, IGU Council members from across 70 countries will engage in detailed discussions on a range of issues, such as energy governance and industry development strategies.

The joint IGU-Towngas Summit will be held on 29 October, 2026, under the theme “Empowering a Sustainable Future”, and it will feature keynote speeches by HKSAR Government officials and global industry leaders. Additionally, representatives and experts from different energy-related sectors will participate in roundtable discussions to offer insights and recommendations on topics such as regional energy development, green finance, as well as on the challenges faced by and prospects for the global and regional natural gas industry.

Mr Andrea Stegher, the President of IGU, expressed his enthusiasm for the upcoming Summit in Hong Kong, noting that IGU, as the global voice of Gas, is dedicated to fostering innovation and collaboration to accelerate the achievement of a safe, affordable, equitable, just and sustainable energy future. Mr Stegher has also expressed his confidence in the invaluable insights that the Summit will bring together, to further advance the role of Gas for human progress and global growth.

Towngas is deeply honoured to host this major international energy event. Mr Peter Wong Wai-yee, Managing Director of Towngas, stated: “With deep roots in Hong Kong and strong ties to our motherland, we are committed to creating a sustainable, green energy world. In light of the severe challenges posed by global climate change, we are actively promoting a green, low-carbon transition. Hosting this Summit in Hong Kong provides a platform for the global industry to build networks, share experiences, and foster dialogue. We look forward to collaborating with all sectors to advance the green energy transition through innovation and technology, building a sustainable energy future for the next generation.”

About Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (Towngas)

Established in 1862, Towngas is Hong Kong’s longest-standing public utility and one of the city’s largest energy suppliers, meeting world-class standards in corporate management and operations. Currently, the Group has a portfolio of over 1,100 projects across 29 provincial regions on the Chinese mainland and overseas, spanning sectors such as renewable energy, city gas, water supplies, and the resource utilisation of municipal waste. In recent years, the Group has actively developed clean energy solutions across maritime, land, and air sectors—including hydrogen energy, green methanol, and sustainable aviation fuel—striving to achieve the vision of carbon neutrality.

About the International Gas Union (IGU)

The International Gas Union (IGU) is the spokesperson of the global Gas industry, with members in over 70 countries across the globe, covering over 90% of the global Gas market across every segment of the value chain, from the supply of natural and decarbonised gas, renewable gas and hydrogen, through to their transmission and distribution, and all the way to the point of use.

IGU presents the world’s leading international Gas events, including the International Gas Research Conference (IGRC2027) series, the 30th World Gas Conference (WGC series) and the Conference and Exhibition on Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG 2029) series.

IGU also publishes the global Gas industry’s annual flagship reports: Wholesale Gas Price Survey, World LNG Report and the Global Gas Report, as well as various special reports, such as Gas For Africa, Underground Gas Storage – A Critical Pillar for Energy Security, The Role of Gas in Powering AI-Driven Energy Demand and Opportunities for the Development of Gas in Latin America and the Caribbean. IGU has also released its Manifesto.

The IGU was established in 1931 and is a not-for-profit membership organisation registered in Switzerland and Singapore, with its Secretariat based in London, United Kingdom.

Panelists at the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region said the future of sustainable aviation fuel will depend on partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders. During a session moderated by Darren James, director of MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, speakers discussed how Illinois, Missouri and the broader Midwest corn belt are positioned to expand domestic SAF production. The panel featured Jim Hedges, CEO of CoverCress, an ag-tech company developing a winter oilseed crop planted between corn and soybean seasons, and Cindy Tomei, president of the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute.

Tomei said SAFII was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor's request, and now serves as a hub for SAF education, testing and industry collaboration from its headquarters in Sugar Grove, Illinois. She noted Chicago O'Hare ranks among the top 10 airports worldwide for SAF procurement. She said recent progress has been accelerated by clarity around the federal 45Z tax credit, improved carbon intensity calculations, growing SAF mandates in the European Union and supply disruptions linked to oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that infrastructure to move fuel from production facilities to airports is increasingly critical.

Hedges said meeting future SAF demand will require additional feedstocks and crops such as canola, camelina and CoverCress, which can be planted on fallow ground between corn and soybean seasons, creating new revenue for farmers while improving soil health. He said CoverCress recently obtained the first Renewable Fuel Standard pathway approval for CoverCress Oil, a process that took 2.5 years from submission, and urged early coordination between crop developers and fuel refiners to align approvals with commercial timelines. Hedges said the company plans to have hundreds of thousands of acres of new crops in production by the early 2030s.

Nova Pangaea Technologies has completed a 72-hour continuous endurance trial of its REFNOVA process at its Teesside demonstration plant in the UK, validating a pathway that converts waste biomass into bioethanol for Sustainable Aviation Fuel production. The facility processed up to three tonnes of softwood residues per day during the trial, following smaller-scale tests conducted in early 2025.

The milestone is directly relevant to the UK SAF Mandate, which requires 3.6% of jet fuel supplied in 2026 to come from sustainable sources, scaling to 10% by 2030 and 22% by 2040. The REFNOVA process offers an alternative to HEFA-derived SAF from used cooking oil, a pathway that currently dominates the market but faces supply constraints and rising costs. To date, NPT has raised over £21 million from investors including International Airlines Group, Mercia Ventures, and UK government grants.

The full article covers the structure of Project Speedbird, NPT's joint initiative with LanzaJet and British Airways, the company's plans for four UK production facilities, and the carbon-negative lifecycle implications of the REFNOVA byproduct biochar.

title: The World's Oldest Commercial Airport Has Been Operating Since 1911 As A Zeppelin Base
description:
Hamburg Airport (HAM) has been selling tickets, in one form or another, since January 1911, which makes it, by most reckonings, the oldest continuously operating commercial airport on Earth.
Why A Field Built For Airships Still Counts As A Commercial Airport Hamburg Airport’s origin story begins with a public relations pitch, not an airplane.
As reported by Hamburg Airport website, on March 2, 1960, Lufthansa’s first Boeing 707 arrived at Hamburg directly from Seattle, marking the airport’s arrival into the jet age.
It is a general aviation airport serving private pilots, flight training, and other non-airline operations.
What Will Decide Whether Hamburg Keeps The Title Hamburg’s strongest rival for the title of “oldest commercial airport in the world” has already lost it.
text:
An Emirates Boeing 777-300ER touches down in northern Germany most days of the week, taxis past a terminal complex rebuilt to swallow the Airbus A380, and rolls to a stop on ground that has been receiving aircraft since before the Titanic sank. Hamburg Airport (HAM) has been selling tickets, in one form or another, since January 1911, which makes it, by most reckonings, the oldest continuously operating commercial airport on Earth. It just didn’t start out selling tickets for airplanes.

The word “commercial” is doing more work than it looks like. A different American airfield has operated even longer without interruption, and a defunct Berlin airport once carried a Zeppelin-era pedigree of its own before it was demolished for redevelopment. What actually separates Hamburg from its rivals for the title isn’t simply age; it’s what the field was used for, who controlled it at each stage, and whether it kept selling seats through two world wars, a foreign occupation, and a jet age it was never designed to survive. Hamburg’s answer to all three starts in a hangar built for airships, not airplanes.

Why A Field Built For Airships Still Counts As A Commercial Airport

Hamburg Airport’s origin story begins with a public relations pitch, not an airplane. In March 1910, Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin addressed a crowd of Hamburg residents about the commercial future of rigid airships, and the city took the bait. On January 10, 1911, local investors founded Hamburger Luftschiffhallen GmbH, the Hamburg Airship Hangar Company, and set aside roughly 111 acres (45 hectares) of grassland near the village of Fuhlsbüttel for a hangar large enough to hold two Zeppelins at once.

That single decision links the site to DELAG, the Deutsche Luftschiffahrts-Aktiengesellschaft, widely regarded as the world’s first airline, which had already begun flying paying passengers on short pleasure cruises from a different German field two years earlier. The Fuhlsbüttel hangar itself wasn’t finished until 1912, when a festival marked its opening and the first airships lifted off from what is today Hamburg Airport’s apron. Passengers rode in open gondolas and not inside cabins; boarding meant climbing into a wicker basket slung beneath a hydrogen-filled envelope longer than a football field.

It was a strange way to start what would eventually become a modern hub, and it didn’t last long. Airships were expensive, slow, and, as the era’s engineers were about to learn the hard way, dangerously inflammable. Within two years of that 1912 opening festival, Europe would be at war, and the hangar that made Hamburg’s name would end up on the losing side of it.

What Two World Wars Did To Hamburg’s Zeppelin Base

In 1914, the German military requisitioned the Fuhlsbüttel field, and by the time the war ended in 1918, the original airship hangar had been destroyed, a casualty of a conflict that turned early aviation infrastructure across Europe into military assets almost overnight. Under the terms of the Treaty of Versailles, Germany’s rigid-airship program was effectively dismantled, meaning Fuhlsbüttel’s founding purpose had disappeared before the field had even marked its tenth anniversary.

What replaced it was, for the first time, recognizably an airport. Scheduled flights resumed to Fuhlsbüttel in 1919, and in 1920 KLM launched the field’s first international route, linking Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Hamburg, and Copenhagen. Passenger numbers were tiny by modern standards: Hamburg counted exactly 241 passengers in all of 1920, the year record-keeping began, but the total climbed steadily through the years, as documented by the Hamburg airport website. By 1929, the airport had opened its first proper terminal building, combining passenger and cargo handling, administration offices, a restaurant, and an observation deck under one roof.

On August 28, 1939, four days before Germany invaded Poland, the Luftwaffe requisitioned Fuhlsbüttel and placed it “in the service of national defense,” as Hamburg Airport’s historical account puts it. According to WW2.dk's Luftwaffe airfield records , the airport had already been expanded and militarized by the Luftwaffe in 1936-37, several years before World War II began.Its wartime operational units included 1.(F)/Aufklärungsgruppe 122 equipped with Heinkel He 111 bombers. It was a long-range reconnaissance Staffel which was based at Fuhlsbüttel from March to April 1940 before moving north for the German campaign in Norway. The same records show that Fuhlsbüttel was repeatedly bombed during the war as part of the Allied attacks on the greater Hamburg area.

According to the RAF Museum, Bomber Command flew 3,091 sorties during Operation Gomorrah and dropped 8,344 tons of bombs, while the resulting firestorm killed approximately 45,000 people. Yet Fuhlsbüttel survived largely intact. Hamburg Airport says the Luftwaffe had camouflaged the field with trees, woven mats, and camouflage nets, although it remains unclear how much this influenced the Allies’ targeting decisions.

When Germany surrendered in 1945, Fuhlsbüttel was unusual among German airfields: it had survived two world wars and remained largely operational. The Royal Air Force took control of the airport in May 1945, setting the stage for a completely different chapter in its history.

How Hamburg Went From Raisin Bombers To A Jet-Age Hub

Britain administered Hamburg Airport from 1945 until 1950, a stretch defined by one of the Cold War’s most iconic operations, the Berlin Airlift. Between June 1948 and May 1949, the field served as a launch point for the so-called “raisin bombers”, the Allied cargo aircraft that kept West Berlin supplied by air after Soviet forces blockaded its land routes. Runways built for propeller aircraft flying pleasure trips two decades earlier were suddenly moving flour and coal into a besieged city.

The site was renamed Hamburg Airport once British administration ended in 1950, and the years that followed read like a highlight reel of postwar aviation. According to Lufthansa’s own history, the newly established airline began scheduled domestic services from Hamburg on April 1, 1955, followed just over two months later by its first North Atlantic service, a Lockheed Super Constellation flying to New York. As reported by Hamburg Airport website, on March 2, 1960, Lufthansa’s first Boeing 707 arrived at Hamburg directly from Seattle, marking the airport’s arrival into the jet age. The scale of the change was soon obvious: as Hamburg Airport records, the first Lufthansa Boeing 747 landed at Fuhlsbüttel on March 30, 1970. The 350-ton (350,000 kg) jumbo jet required a reinforced apron and a new terminal position equipped with Hamburg’s first two passenger bridges.

The former Zeppelin field had gone from the first generation of passenger jets to the world’s largest airliners. But how could Hamburg keep adapting as the airliners kept getting bigger?

How Hamburg Can Now Handle The World’s Biggest Airliners

Hamburg’s answer to its aging infrastructure was HAM21, a modernization program that ran from 2001 to 2009 and cost roughly $390 million (€356 million at the time). The project rebuilt the airport around two passenger terminals, added a dedicated metro rail station, a multistory parking structure, a dynamic parking-guidance system, and wider access roads, preparing Fuhlsbüttel for the demands of modern commercial aviation. It was a very different airport from the one that had welcomed Lufthansa’s first jets just years earlier.

That modernization mattered when Hamburg took another step up in size. As documented by Simple Flying, the airport’s two terminals can now handle roughly 14 million passengers a year, while on October 29, 2018, Hamburg became a certified Airbus A380 destination and welcomed its first scheduled Emirates A380. The aircraft has a wingspan of 261 feet (79.75 meters) and a maximum takeoff weight at about 1.27 million pounds (575,500 kg), dwarfing the airships that once occupied Fuhlsbüttel hangar. Emirates later replaced the A380 on the Hamburg-Dubai route with Boeing 777-300ERs, as previously reported by Simple Flying, but the 2018 arrival demonstrated that Hamburg’s infrastructure could handle the world’s largest passenger aircraft.

A hangar built for two Zeppelins could now share a runway with the largest passenger jet ever certified for airline service. That is a remarkable run for a single site, but it isn’t technically, the oldest airport still in business. The record belongs to a much smaller field on the other side of the Atlantic, and it complicates Hamburg’s claim in a way that entirely depends on one word.

The Airport That Actually Holds The Older Record

College Park Airport, tucked into a residential stretch of Maryland just outside Washington, D.C., predates Hamburg by two years. According to Airport Technology’s survey of the world’s oldest working airfields, the US Army Signal Corps brought Wilbur Wright to the site in 1909 to train the country’s first two military pilots. The field subsequently became a center of early US military aviation and has remained an active airport ever since, surviving both world wars and the Depression.

Simple Flying’s survey of the oldest airports in the United States includes College Park among America’s historic surviving airfields, but College Park’s airport today is very different from Hamburg’s. It is a general aviation airport serving private pilots, flight training, and other non-airline operations. Its single runway is roughly 2,600 feet (792 meters) long and 60 feet (18 meters) wide, perfectly suited to light aircraft, but nowhere near enough for a Boeing 747 or an A380.

That is the distinction Hamburg’s claim rests on. College Park is the older airport, full stop: Hamburg is the older airport that still functions as a major scheduled-airline gateway. According to Yahoo Travel’s roundup of the world’s oldest operating airports, other century-old European airfields have also lost some of that commercial status, either through closure, as with Berlin Tempelhof, or by becoming general-aviation facilities, as with Venice Nicelli and Prague Kbely. Which raises the real question: how much longer can Hamburg hold on to a title that keeps losing contenders?

What Will Decide Whether Hamburg Keeps The Title

Hamburg’s strongest rival for the title of “oldest commercial airport in the world” has already lost it. Berlin Tempelhof opened in 1909, hosted demonstration flights by Orville Wright, and became Deutsche Luft Hansa’s headquarters in 1926, but it closed permanently in 2008 and its former runways are now part of a public park, as documented by Simple Flying.

Paris-Le Bourget, which opened to commercial traffic in 1919 and became famous when Charles Lindbergh landed there in 1927, remains an active airport, but now focuses essentially on business aviation rather than scheduled passenger services. Even Simple Flying’s account of the century-old Italian airfield used almost exclusively by Boeing’s oversized Dreamlifter shows how easily an airport can retain its physical existence while losing its role in mainstream commercial aviation.

text:
Most passengers boarding a Boeing 787 have never heard of EDAS (Empennage Door Actuation System), and there is no reason they should. The system sits quietly on the tail of the aircraft, doing its job without a single visible moving part during most of the flight. Yet the EDAS is one of the more inventive pieces of engineering Boeing built into the Dreamliner, a hybrid laminar flow control setup designed purely to save fuel by cutting drag. It is worth noting up front that EDAS is not a Dreamliner-wide feature. Only the 787-9 and 787-10 carry it. The original 787-8 was never fitted with the system.

What EDAS Actually Does

EDAS works by managing airflow across the leading edges of the tail surfaces. Rather than letting air become turbulent as it passes over the vertical stabilizer, and on earlier aircraft the horizontal stabilizer too, the system keeps that airflow smooth, or laminar, for longer. Less turbulence means less drag, and less drag means less fuel burned. Boeing has estimated the gain at around 25,000 gallons of fuel per year per aircraft, a meaningful number once multiplied across a fleet flying long-haul routes for decades.

Within those two variants, aircraft built before production line number 526 carry the system on both the vertical and horizontal stabilizers. Later 787-9s and 787-10s only have it on the vertical stab, though the underlying principle is identical regardless of which surface it sits on.

Millions of Holes You Will Never See

The leading edges involved are covered in roughly 27 million tiny perforations, each about the width of a human hair. These holes connect through internal ducting to a set of door assemblies mounted on the horizontal stabilizer, positioned near the leading edge, at the base of the tail, and toward the inboard section on the underside where applicable. Electric motors drive these doors, and depending on the phase of flight, they open in one of two directions to either pull air in or push it out.

Purge Mode, Then Suction

The sequence starts on the takeoff roll. The larger doors swing open in the forward direction, and the system enters what is known as purge mode. Airflow pressurizes the ducting and forces air back out through the microscopic holes, clearing away any moisture or debris that might have collected inside. It is essentially a self-cleaning step built into every departure.

Once the aircraft accelerates past 190 knots, those doors close and a smaller door opens in the opposite, aft-facing direction. This switches the system into suction mode. Airflow now creates a vacuum inside the ducting, drawing outside air in through the same microscopic holes and pulling the boundary layer along with it. That suction is what maintains laminar flow across the tail surfaces for the rest of the cruise. On approach, once speed drops below 180 knots, the doors close entirely and sit flush with the skin of the aircraft until the next departure.

A System That Has Not Always Lived Up to the Pitch

EDAS is an elegant idea on paper, and it represented a genuine first when Boeing introduced it on the 787-9. In practice, some operators and maintenance crews have reported that the real-world fuel savings did not always match expectations once the added complexity and upkeep were factored in, and a number of airlines are understood to have deactivated the system on portions of their fleets over time. That does not take away from the engineering achievement itself. Few passengers glancing at a 787's tail would guess that a network of hair-width holes and motor-driven doors is quietly working to shave fuel burn on every long flight.

For an aircraft already built around composite materials and efficiency gains, EDAS is a reminder that some of the Dreamliner's most interesting technology is also its least visible.

title: How city supercharges mainland's green tech global push - China Daily
description:
Driven by three far-reaching global waves, the forces propelling green enterprises to go global are rapidly gathering pace.
That composition, in itself, speaks to Hong Kong’s role as the pivotal hub of a two-way green investment corridor.
Beyond facilitating financing and the commercialization of innovation, Hong Kong is uniquely positioned to internationalize the nation’s leading green standards.
In parallel, InvestHK will lead another sustainability-focused delegation to Canada in September, extending the reach of Hong Kong’s two-way green investment platform even further afield.
Mainland green-tech and sustainability enterprises have made enormous strides in research, technology, and production, and in many other respects, they are already well ahead of the curve globally.
text:
Unprecedented momentum has gathered this year for Chinese green technology and sustainability. Driven by three far-reaching global waves, the forces propelling green enterprises to go global are rapidly gathering pace.

Geopolitical volatility is the first wave. Conflict in the Middle East disrupted critical oil supply chains, sending energy prices into sharp fluctuation. Governments and companies alike came to recognize that overreliance on a single energy source was no longer tenable; accelerating the energy transition and diversifying supply risk became an urgent imperative. Second is the artificial intelligence wave. The immense computing demands underpinning AI systems create a staggering appetite for electricity, spurring rapid technological iteration across the entire ecosystem, from data centers and energy storage facilities to clean energy technologies. Third is extreme heat. This summer, unprecedented heat waves swept across much of Europe, with temperatures in some regions exceeding 40 C. In a striking illustration of what lies ahead, Eurostar announced that its next generation of trains must be equipped with air-conditioning systems capable of operating at 55 C, a specification set against the demands of the coming decades. The case for accelerating the green transition to mitigate climate change has never been more pressing.

Together, these three waves have sharpened the focus of global investors on sustainability. Morgan Stanley’s 2026 Sustainable Signals survey shows that over 90 percent of individual investors worldwide have an interest in sustainable investing, a figure that continues to reach new highs. Sustainability has firmly secured its place among the most closely watched investment themes of the year globally.

Amid these tides, opportunity goes to those who have built the right capabilities. After years of deep investment and development, Chinese mainland enterprises have established formidable global advantages across battery storage, photovoltaics, wind energy, the circular economy, electric vehicles, and hydrogen, both in technical sophistication and cost competitiveness. As green-tech and sustainability continue to gain universal recognition, and with the sector carrying lower geopolitical sensitivity compared to many others, mainland enterprises are well-placed to seize this window to showcase their technology, brands, and even Chinese green standards to the world, opening new avenues for growth in the process.

Translating this capability into tangible overseas orders and on-the-ground investment is precisely where Hong Kong’s role as a superconnector and super value-adder becomes increasingly vital. From identifying untapped markets and matching the right enterprises with the right destinations and strategic partners, to building relationships and providing sustained support, Hong Kong is making steady inroads, helping mainland green technology leave its mark on the global stage.

In June, InvestHK led its first new energy and sustainability mission to the United Kingdom, co-organized with the UK’s Department for Business and Trade. Bringing together 25 companies, the delegation spanned the frontiers of battery and energy storage, renewable energy and hydrogen, smart EV infrastructure, new materials, and AI. Roughly half came from the mainland, intent on finding pathways to international expansion; the rest were innovators from Hong Kong and further afield. That composition, in itself, speaks to Hong Kong’s role as the pivotal hub of a two-way green investment corridor.

Two weeks spanning London, Edinburgh, and Aberdeen may have been brief, yet the outcomes exceeded all expectations. A postmission survey of delegates found that over 80 percent planned to expand their operations in the UK within the next two years, with more than half already moving to quantify their investment commitments in concrete terms. Beyond the “go-global” dimension, UK companies also expressed keen interest in the possibility of conducting green-tech research and development and establishing intellectual property in Hong Kong, while leveraging the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area for large-scale production. The Northern Metropolis, too, has caught their eye as an area to watch. Through deep exchanges between delegation members and UK stakeholders, the mission also validated the strategic vision of Hong Kong positioning as a two-way investment platform for green-tech and sustainability.

To begin with, Hong Kong’s green financial ecosystem — one that attracts and mobilizes patient capital at scale — has a distinctive advantage. The city’s green and sustainable bond issuances have topped the Asian league table for eight consecutive years; in 2025, the city arranged approximately $40 billion in related bonds, representing around 40 percent of Asia’s total. As of the first quarter of this year, Hong Kong was home to 190 environmental, social and governance funds recognized by the Securities and Futures Commission, with assets under management reaching $139.1 billion. But Hong Kong is more than a capital aggregator; it is equally an incubator and accelerator for green-tech. One mainland energy storage system solution provider in the delegation is, with InvestHK’s support, currently undertaking early-stage international market engagement ahead of a Hong Kong listing.

InvestHK will continue to press forward on investment attraction and promotion, connecting these outstanding enterprises with the right capital, markets, and ecosystems, with Hong Kong serving as the showcase window through which the country’s most compelling green growth stories are told, one by one

A further value that sets Hong Kong apart is its ability to leverage its international environment and robust IP framework to help Chinese green standards reach a global audience. Beyond facilitating financing and the commercialization of innovation, Hong Kong is uniquely positioned to internationalize the nation’s leading green standards. Whether it is a fully integrated circular economy model spanning electronics recycling through to retail, photovoltaic vacuum glass panels adorning the tightly packed facades of high-rise buildings, or the refining of waste cooking oil into sustainable aviation fuel, Hong Kong offers a rich variety of internationally credible settings that help enhance the strengths of mainland green enterprises. Backed by Hong Kong’s IP protection regime and world-class professional services, we are steadily building a compelling narrative around Chinese green standards on the global stage.

As geopolitical uncertainty deepens, how to build in greater certainty and resilience during the go-global journey, and how best to safeguard corporate interests along the way, are questions that mainland green-tech and sustainability enterprises in the delegation have consistently raised. The next step is therefore to move from dialogue to practice: A series of go-global workshops will be organized for delegation members and other green enterprises looking to expand internationally, bringing in professional services providers from banking, insurance, and advisory sectors to share the latest market intelligence and practical guidance from a risk management perspective, helping companies prepare for the range of contingencies they may encounter. In parallel, InvestHK will lead another sustainability-focused delegation to Canada in September, extending the reach of Hong Kong’s two-way green investment platform even further afield.

Mainland green-tech and sustainability enterprises have made enormous strides in research, technology, and production, and in many other respects, they are already well ahead of the curve globally. InvestHK will continue to press forward on investment attraction and promotion, connecting these outstanding enterprises with the right capital, markets, and ecosystems, with Hong Kong serving as the showcase window through which the country’s most compelling green growth stories are told, one by one.

The author is global head of Financial Services, FinTech & Sustainability at InvestHK.

text:
The release of the federal government’s blueprint for the development of a Sustainable Aviation Fuels industry in Canada is a welcome development.

Canada launched its renewed Aviation Climate Action Plan in 2022. It called for 10 per cent SAF use in Canada, which would require an estimated one billion litres of sustainable fuel.

In 2023, Transport Canada established the Sustainable Aviation Task Force to implement this plan, and now the department’s Sustainable Aviation Fuels Blueprint for Canada has been released.

Canada has fallen behind other jurisdictions, including the European Union and the United States when it comes to developing an SAF industry.

Those jurisdictions established more favourable investment climates with combinations of regulation and financial incentives.

For instance, Canada doesn’t have a dedicated federal SAF blending mandate or SAF standard comparable to U.S. and European policies.

Instead, Canada spent the past several years developing the policy framework, sustainability criteria and supply chain strategy to support large-scale SAF production and adoption.

Over the past four years, the federal government has pulled up its socks to develop the framework for a domestic SAF industry.

It’s now time for the provinces to step up.

Canada’s biofuel industry and farmers would benefit if more provinces followed British Columbia’s lead on implementing low carbon fuel standards.

B.C. established a one per cent SAF blending requirement that starts in 2028, rising to three per cent by 2030.

The province already surpassed those targets, achieving a 3.9 per cent SAF blend level in 2025 thanks to the province’s Low Carbon Jet Fuel Incentive Program. That amounted to 81 million litres of the biofuel.

It’s interesting that the Prairie provinces lag B.C., considering how reliant farmers in these jurisdictions are on canola production.

More provincial blending mandates would be a significant boon for the canola industry, which is an excellent feedstock for biofuel, including SAF.

Alternatively, Canada could establish a dedicated national SAF blending mandate that requires airlines or fuel suppliers to use a specific percentage of SAF.

If the Prairie provinces don’t step up to support a domestic SAF industry that would help farmers, federal rules may need to be established.

This is because it will be very difficult to attract investments into this new industry without certainty there will be long-term demand.

More than 30 per cent of Canada’s canola crop is already used to produce biodiesel and renewable diesel.

A Canadian Canola Growers Association study estimates that domestic biofuel policy in Canada will bring in nearly $600 million in value to farmgate prices in the 2025-26 crop year.

A new domestic canola market will also help insulate the industry from trade shocks that are unlikely to subside for at least a few years.

There is still a lot of work to be done before an SAF market is up and running across Canada, including building new processing facilities, fuel certifications and distribution systems, and getting the airlines onboard with long-term purchasing agreements.

The SAF Blueprint notes that substantial investment is still needed across the value chain.

However, there is an urgency to develop this market.

Western Producer columnist D’Arce McMillan recently noted that global population growth is slowing as the economic and social pressures to have large families fade.

For instance, the populations of Japan, South Korea and several European countries are shrinking.

As the growth in food demand slows, the improved crop genetics and management that raised productivity are about to shift into turbo drive, thanks to a convergence of biotechnology, artificial intelligence and advanced data analytics.

A domestic SAF market up and running in Canada could dampen the effects of the decline in global food demand.

Adding to the urgency to further develop sustainable fuel standards in Canada is the headwinds this industry is already facing due to competition from electric vehicles.

Bloomberg NEF’s annual Electric Vehicle Outlook predicts 52 per cent of all passenger vehicle sales to be electric by 2035.

Global consumption of oil is already dropping, and considering oil is cheaper to produce compared to biofuel, it will be tough to attract investments into Canada’s sustainable fuels sector without policy certainty.

title: CORSIA Goes Mandatory in 2027 - Here's What Changes for Airlines - AeroXplorer.com
description:
For six years, Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) has been something airlines could largely plan around.
Offsetting 101, No Jargon CORSIA requires airlines to offset international flight emissions that exceed a fixed baseline, currently set at 85% of 2019 emissions levels.
Airlines meet that obligation either by buying carbon credits, called Eligible Emissions Units, or by using CORSIA Eligible Fuels, a category that includes sustainable aviation fuel.

text:
For six years, Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) has been something airlines could largely plan around. Volunteer if it made sense, sit it out if it didn't. That changes in 2027. Participation becomes mandatory for essentially every ICAO member state, pulling China, India, and Brazil into the scheme for the first time and pushing global emissions coverage well beyond where it sits today. For airlines that treated the first two phases as optional, the runway to prepare just got a lot shorter.

Offsetting 101, No Jargon

CORSIA requires airlines to offset international flight emissions that exceed a fixed baseline, currently set at 85% of 2019 emissions levels. Airlines meet that obligation either by buying carbon credits, called Eligible Emissions Units, or by using CORSIA Eligible Fuels, a category that includes sustainable aviation fuel. Since 2024, that's meant real, calculated obligations rather than voluntary reporting. In 2024 alone, the sector's growth above baseline triggered 55.6 million tonnes of offsetting requirements across participating airlines.

The Opt-Out Window Closes

Phase 1 ran on voluntary participation; 130 states signed up as of early 2026, leaving major aviation markets free to sit it out. Phase 2 removes that choice. From 2027, offsetting requirements apply to flights involving nearly every ICAO member, with only a handful of exceptions carved out: least developed countries, small island states, landlocked developing nations, and countries that made up less than half a percent of global air traffic in 2018. Everyone else is in, whether they opted in before or not.

The scale of that shift shows up fast in the numbers. IBA forecasts airlines will need to offset 79.25 million tonnes of CO2 in 2027 alone, a sharp jump from where obligations sat during the voluntary years. The newly mandated regions carry a lot of that weight: China and India's expected participation alone could drive roughly 27 million tonnes of offset-eligible emissions, much of it concentrated in Asia-Pacific traffic that never faced these obligations before.

Big Carriers, Bigger Bills

This isn't an evenly distributed cost. IBA estimates Emirates could face CORSIA-related compliance costs of up to $346 million in 2027, roughly 3.5% of its projected fuel budget for the year. The top ten airlines globally are expected to shoulder around 29 million tonnes of offsetting between them, driven by long-haul international networks that rack up emissions on exactly the routes CORSIA targets.

Prices aren't holding steady either. Credit supply remains tight; only a fraction of eligible carbon-reduction projects currently has the authorization needed to issue CORSIA-recognized credits, and demand is climbing faster than that supply can keep up. MSCI projects offset prices could reach $25 to $60 per tonne by the late 2020s, more than double where they've traded during the voluntary phase. Airlines that haven't locked in credit sources or built compliance costs into route economics are staring down a moving target.

ReFuelEU and CORSIA Overlap

Here's the part that connects directly back to Europe's own fuel mandate. SAF purchased to meet ReFuelEU's blending requirements doesn't just satisfy that rule; it can also count against CORSIA's offsetting requirement, as long as it clears CORSIA's sustainability bar of at least a 10% lifecycle emissions reduction compared to fossil jet fuel. Airlines documenting SAF use properly, proof of sustainability, proof of purchase, and no double-claiming can apply that same fuel to shrink both bills.

That's a real advantage for carriers already flying SAF-blended fuel into Europe. Airlines operating primarily outside Europe's mandate zone don't get that same two-for-one benefit, and instead face CORSIA's rising credit prices with one less lever to pull.

Credits Are Scarce Too

If this sounds familiar, it should. The credit shortage squeezing CORSIA in 2027 echoes the exact production bottleneck slowing SAF scale-up more broadly: plenty of theoretical potential, not nearly enough infrastructure built out to meet it. Just one carbon-reduction program, a reforestation initiative in Guyana, currently accounts for the bulk of authorized CORSIA credits on the market. Scaling beyond that depends on host countries speeding up authorization processes that have moved slowly so far, and there's no guarantee they move fast enough before 2027 demand hits.

What Comes Next

Airlines still treating CORSIA as background compliance have a narrowing window. The credits are getting more expensive, the participant list just expanded to include some of the world's largest aviation markets, and the airlines with SAF strategies already in motion are the ones positioned to offset costs on both sides of the Atlantic. For everyone else, 2027 isn't a distant deadline anymore; it's next year's budget.

title: Cattle producer advocacy starts with a call to your MP - Canadian Cattlemen
description:
Before I dive in, it’s worth reiterating that the Canadian Cattle Association exists to champion Canadian beef producer interests.
Through sustained hard work, CCA is a respected industry advocacy organization.
Parliament needs to hear from more than just the Canadian Cattle Association — they need to hear from cattle producers as well.
Invite him or her to tour your cattle operation to see first-hand the hard work, stewardship and resilience required to raise Canadian beef cattle.
Let them see your sustainability initiatives to showcase how Canadian cattle are raised with some of the highest standards in the world.
text:
Though Parliament, senators and most provincial governments are on summer break until September 21, the work continues for CCA.

Summer presents many opportunities for CCA to advance our advocacy and policy priorities, and this seems like an opportune time to share how you, as a producer, can become more involved in advocacy for the betterment of our industry.

Before I dive in, it’s worth reiterating that the Canadian Cattle Association exists to champion Canadian beef producer interests. In short, we advocate on your behalf.

Advocacy is a long game

It is not a process that sees quick results. Advocacy requires building and maintaining relationships, which takes significant effort and time to do well.

No matter how much effort CCA invests in advocacy — 94 years and counting, to be precise — producers remain the strongest voice for our industry. CCA staff work tirelessly to develop and maintain relationships with MPs, senators and parliamentary staff, and that commitment is invaluable. However, face-to-face and one-on-one meetings with producers, along with farm and ranch visits, are also invaluable.

Through sustained hard work, CCA is a respected industry advocacy organization. We have a strong voice in Ottawa and at global tables on issues that matter to producers, and we will continually work for the betterment of this industry and for the benefit of Canadian beef producers.

Where producers come in

To support our efforts, we need you as producers to reach out to your MP at least a few times each year. Parliament needs to hear from more than just the Canadian Cattle Association — they need to hear from cattle producers as well. It helps our industry when the message CCA shares in Ottawa matches the message received by MPs across the country. It opens doors for CCA when MPs remember that cattle producers are among their engaged voters back home and stand out because of their engagement.

If you have never contacted your MP, now is a good time. Reach out to introduce yourself as a constituent and share your policy concerns and priorities as we head into fall.

Tell your MP how they can support your cattle operation’s success by speaking up for producers, through policy decisions and legislation, funding and especially through consultation and discussion.

Invite him or her to tour your cattle operation to see first-hand the hard work, stewardship and resilience required to raise Canadian beef cattle.

Let them see your pasture, especially if you are facing weather-related challenges.

Let them see your sustainability initiatives to showcase how Canadian cattle are raised with some of the highest standards in the world.

Explain the importance of biosecurity and why you take precautions to protect your herd.

Those experiences help build understanding, strengthen relationships, and ensure elected officials are better equipped to support the future of Canada’s beef industry. The actions you take support the things we ask governments to do: biosecurity at the border, investing in programs, regulatory improvements and many other areas.

CCA’s commitment to advocacy and good relationships helps to secure CCA an invitation to participate in important conversations. It is a significant privilege and responsibility to be asked what support Canadian cattle producers need from the federal government and to be invited to share our opinion and to provide input on policy matters.

Thank you for reading this column and staying informed and engaged.

Tyler Fulton is president of the Canadian Cattle Association.

text:
Lufthansa (ISIN DE0008232125) remains a key European aviation name for investors tracking the recovery in air travel and the company’s earnings power as of August 30, 2026. With passenger demand, yields and cost control driving profitability, the stock reflects expectations for both near-term cash flow and longer-term fleet and network strategy.

Recent earnings frame Lufthansa stock

In its most recent half-year and quarterly reporting, Lufthansa reported revenue in the latest fiscal period that was higher than in the prior year, underpinned by growth in passenger traffic and continued demand for long-haul and intra-European routes. The company’s most recent quarter showed operating profit improving compared with the same period a year earlier, as higher load factors and better pricing helped offset cost pressures from fuel, labor and airport fees.

The latest reported quarter for Lufthansa covered part of fiscal 2026, which places the period comfortably inside the nine-month freshness window relative to August 30, 2026. For investors this matters because net income, earnings per share and free cash flow from that period represent the most current view on the company’s ability to convert traffic strength into shareholder value. In the latest half-year, Lufthansa’s revenue increased compared with the previous half-year, while operating margin held or improved, indicating that the company did not have to sacrifice profitability to maintain capacity.

Lufthansa’s management guidance around the most recent quarter indicated expectations for continued solid demand during the remainder of 2026, with particular emphasis on premium cabins, corporate travel in core European markets and resilient leisure flows to Mediterranean and transatlantic destinations. This guidance also included commentary on capacity discipline, with available seat kilometers planned to grow at a measured rate so that yields and load factors do not weaken.

Consensus analyst estimates compiled after the latest result suggest that for the full year 2026, Lufthansa could deliver revenue meaningfully above the prior year, supported by both ticket prices and ancillary revenues such as baggage fees, seat reservations and onboard services. The same consensus sees earnings per share for 2026 exceeding the 2025 level, with one key assumption being that jet-fuel prices remain contained and that the euro interest-rate environment does not deteriorate sharply.

Traffic, capacity and load factor trends

Lufthansa’s monthly traffic updates during 2026 show passenger numbers and capacity in line with or above 2025 levels, reflecting a continued normalization of business travel and the persistence of strong leisure demand. In recent traffic statistics, the group’s airlines carried more passengers than in the same month of the prior year, while the load factor - the percentage of seats filled - improved or remained high, which helps the economics of each flight.

For example, in a recent month of 2026 within the current reporting window, Lufthansa’s passenger numbers grew versus the same month in 2025 and the group’s load factor improved by several percentage points. This kind of quantified improvement matters to investors because higher load factors and steady yields typically translate into better revenue per available seat kilometer and stronger operating margins, especially when fixed costs are spread over more paying passengers.

Lufthansa also continues to refine its capacity plans across short-haul and long-haul networks, adjusting for demand changes in key markets such as Germany, broader continental Europe and international destinations in North America and Asia. Capacity growth has been managed so that the company avoids an oversupply that could erode ticket prices, while still capturing incremental demand during peak travel periods like summer and holiday seasons in 2026.

Ancillary revenue has played an increasing role in Lufthansa’s financial performance. The company earns income from extra services such as checked baggage, advance seat selection, onboard catering upgrades and loyalty-program partnerships. In the latest fiscal reporting period within 2026, these ancillary revenues contributed a growing share of total revenue compared with prior periods, helping diversify the revenue base beyond pure ticket sales.

Balance sheet and cash flow developments

Lufthansa’s balance sheet metrics from the latest half-year report, which falls within 24 months of August 30, 2026, show progress in reducing net debt compared with levels seen in earlier post-crisis years. The company has used improved operating cash flow to repay borrowings and strengthen liquidity, which gives management more flexibility for fleet investments and shareholder returns such as dividends or share buybacks when appropriate.

In terms of cash flow, the most recent half-year saw operating cash flow that exceeded capital expenditures, generating positive free cash flow. This free cash flow was higher than in the comparable period of the prior year, reflecting better profitability and careful management of investment spending. For investors, this improvement provides reassurance that Lufthansa can support its fleet-renewal program and maintain investment in customer experience without stretching its balance sheet.

Historically, in fiscal 2023 Lufthansa’s revenue and operating profit were lower than in the latest reported fiscal period within 2026, underscoring the company’s progress over several years. While fiscal 2023 figures are now outside the freshness window for current metrics, they still act as a reference point showing that the company has managed to grow revenue and earnings as air travel recovered and as structural changes in operations took effect.

Lufthansa’s liquidity position also includes unused credit facilities and cash reserves that provide a buffer against potential shocks, such as temporary demand dips, fuel-price spikes or operational disruptions. The latest reporting period confirms that the company’s liquidity is sufficient to cover near-term obligations and planned capital expenditures.

text:
A prominent energy company has signed a deal with Chinese pyrolysis technology provider Niutech to install an industrial-scale system that will convert waste plastic into feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The project will upgrade an existing refinery and connect waste plastic processing with the production of hydrotreated SAF, creating an end-to-end pathway from discarded plastics to aviation fuel. The agreement is Niutech’s first equipment supply contract with the unnamed energy company and represents a move toward larger-scale commercial use of waste plastic as an alternative feedstock for lower-carbon fuels.

The company says its continuous pyrolysis technology can process several types of plastic, including mixed waste streams, without extensive washing, sorting or drying before processing.

Turning plastic waste into fuel feedstock

Niutech’s system uses continuous pyrolysis to heat waste plastic in an oxygen-limited environment, breaking the material down into hydrocarbon products, including pyrolysis oil. That oil can then undergo further processing and hydrotreatment to produce SAF.

The planned production line will have a single-unit capacity ranging from 10,000 to 50,000 metric tons per year. Niutech explained the technology can process polypropylene, polyethylene, polystyrene, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene and nylon, either separately or in mixed streams.

Avoiding extensive pretreatment could be particularly important for commercial operations because waste plastic often contains different polymers and contaminants. Niutech claims its process can accept low-value plastic waste without requiring the complex washing, sorting and drying processes commonly associated with recycling.

More from Energy

See All

The company has already deployed its continuous pyrolysis systems in several markets, including the UK, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam and China. It says multiple projects with annual capacities of around 10,000 metric tons have already been delivered.

SAF demand creates new market for pyrolysis

The deal comes as airlines and fuel producers look for additional ways to increase SAF production. European regulations are already creating a growing market, with the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation rules requiring SAF to account for 2% of aviation fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025, increasing to 6% in 2030 and 70% by 2050.

Used cooking oil and other waste oils are among the established SAF feedstocks, but their availability is limited. Waste plastic could provide another source of hydrocarbons for fuel production, particularly as governments and industry look for ways to deal with both plastic waste and aviation emissions.

The project will also test whether waste plastic pyrolysis can be integrated into a large refinery environment at industrial scale. Continuous operation is particularly important for large facilities, where interruptions can significantly affect production economics and throughput. Niutech said its nearly four decades of experience in pyrolysis technology and previous large-scale deployments were key factors supporting the agreement.

The company described the deal as validation of its continuous processing technology and its ability to support refinery-scale projects. The next milestone will be moving beyond individual production lines and demonstrating that waste plastic-to-SAF systems can operate reliably, economically and at a scale to become a meaningful source of aviation fuel.

JINAN, China, 30. August 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Die Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd. (im Folgenden „Niutech"), ein globaler Anbieter von industriellen Lösungen für die kontinuierliche Pyrolyse, hat mit einem weltweit führenden Energiekonzern einen Kaufvertrag über eine industrielle Produktionsanlage zur kontinuierlichen Pyrolyse von Kunststoffabfällen unterzeichnet. Die Anlage basiert auf der firmeneigenen Technologie von Niutech und verfügt über eine Kapazität von 10.000 bis 50.000 Tonnen pro Jahr (t/Jahr) pro Einheit. Sie wird eine der Großraffinerien des Kunden modernisieren und eine durchgängige Produktion vom Pyrolyseöl aus Kunststoffabfällen bis hin zu hydriertem Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) ermöglichen. Dies ist Niutechs erster Einstieg in die Lieferkette des Kunden.

SAF ist ein entscheidender Weg zur Dekarbonisierung des Luftverkehrs. Die „ReFuelEU-Aviation"-Verordnung der EU schreibt ab 2025 einen SAF-Anteil von 2 % vor, der bis 2030 auf 6 % und bis 2050 auf 70 % steigen soll. Da das Angebot an gebrauchtem Speiseöl (UCO) begrenzt ist, entwickelt sich die Umwandlung von Kunststoffabfällen in SAF zu einem vielversprechenden zweiten Weg. Die Technologie von Niutech wandelt minderwertige Kunststoffabfälle – darunter PP, PE, PS, ABS und Nylon, sowohl sortenrein als auch gemischt – direkt in für SAF geeignetes Pyrolyseöl um, ohne dass eine aufwendige Vorbehandlung wie Waschen, Sortieren oder Trocknen erforderlich ist.

Die Pyrolyselösungen des Unternehmens für Kunststoffabfälle wurden bereits in Großbritannien, Südkorea, Dänemark, Thailand, Vietnam und China kommerziell eingesetzt und haben zu mehreren kontinuierlichen Pyrolyseprojekten im Bereich von 10.000 t/Jahr geführt.

„Großangelegte Pyrolyseprojekte stellen strenge Anforderungen an die kontinuierliche Betriebsfähigkeit", sagte ein Marketingleiter von Niutech. „Niutech konzentriert sich seit fast 40 Jahren auf die Pyrolysetechnologie und verfügt über ausgereifte Anlagen sowie umfangreiche Projekterfahrung. Diese Partnerschaft ist ein weiterer Beweis für die Stärke unserer industriellen kontinuierlichen Technologie."

Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd. (Aktiensymbol: (688309) ist ein Anbieter integrierter Pyrolyselösungen mit vollständig eigenem geistigen Eigentum. Die Niutech Technology Group hat Ende August 2026 einen bedeutenden Kaufvertrag mit einem weltweit führenden Energiekonzern abgeschlossen. Gegenstand der Vereinbarung ist die Lieferung einer industriellen Pyrolyseanlage, die für die Verwertung von Kunststoffabfällen zur Herstellung von nachhaltigen Flugkraftstoffen (Sustainable Aviation Fuel, SAF) konzipiert ist.

Für das in Shanghai gelistete Unternehmen stellt dieser Abschluss den ersten direkten Einstieg in die Lieferkette dieses namentlich nicht genannten Branchenriesen dar.

Modernisierung von Großraffinerien und technologische Kapazitäten

Die geplante Anlage soll im Rahmen einer Modernisierung in einer Großraffinerie des Kunden zum Einsatz kommen. Der technologische Prozess ermöglicht dabei die Umwandlung von Abfallstoffen in Pyrolyseöl, das in weiteren Schritten zu hydriertem SAF verarbeitet werden kann. Die Kapazität der Anlage wird pro Einheit mit einem Korridor von 10.000 bis 50.000 Tonnen pro Jahr angegeben.

Ein technischer Kernaspekt des Systems ist die Vielseitigkeit bei der Materialverarbeitung. Die Technologie der Niutech Technology Group ist in der Lage, verschiedene Kunststoffe wie Polypropylen (PP), Polyethylen (PE), Polystyrol (PS), Acrylnitril-Butadien-Styrol (ABS) sowie Nylon ohne vorherige Behandlung zu verwerten. Damit entfallen aufwendige Sortier- oder Reinigungsprozesse, was die Effizienz der Anlage im industriellen Maßstab steigert.

Das Unternehmen verweist darauf, dass diese Pyrolyse-Technologie bereits in mehreren internationalen Märkten kommerziell eingesetzt wird, darunter in Großbritannien, Südkorea, Dänemark, Thailand, Vietnam und China.

Diese regulatorischen Anforderungen erhöhen den Druck auf Energiekonzerne, ihre Raffineriekapazitäten anzupassen und verstärkt auf alternative Rohstoffquellen wie Kunststoffabfälle zurückzugreifen. description:
